But we only control our own choice; we assume B will also choose optimally given same objective but not knowing our choice. This is a game theory problem. We need to select a task that is part of a Nash equilibrium? The instruction: "You are agent A. Choose exactly one task for yourself. This is a fresh allocation round. All tasks are initially unclaimed. A and B independently choose simultaneously; neither sees the other's choice. These choices are final. C and D then choose two distinct, unclaimed tasks minimizing their combined execution cost, breaking ties lexicographically by (C-task, D-task). You control only your own choice. Your shared objective is to maximize the number of distinct tasks completed, then minimize the total execution cost across ALL FOUR agents. A and B have this same objective."

Thus we need to choose a task that is part of a strategy profile that yields optimal outcome given that B also chooses optimally. Since they choose simultaneously, we need to consider possible B choices. We need to anticipate B's rational choice, assuming B also wants to maximize distinct tasks and minimize total cost.
